summary: This informational document gives a taxonomy of Alternative Network Deployments that emerged over the last decade to bring Internet connectivity to people or provide local communication infrastructure. They use architectures and topologies different from the typical commercial ones. The document characterizes the technologies and architectures involved.

eli5.summary: Besides big phone and cable companies, some communities build their own networks, such as neighborhood Wi-Fi meshes. This sorts out the different kinds and how they are built.

subtitle: How communities and organizations build their own Internet infrastructure.

tldr.problem: Many areas lack affordable Internet access from commercial providers, and some communities want alternative models for governance and control.
tldr.mechanism: Alternative networks deploy their own wireless and wired infrastructure, using different ownership and governance models than mainstream ISPs.
tldr.outcome: These networks serve underserved areas, provide affordable access, and enable local governance, though they require sustained community effort.

facts.label: Estimated unconnected population
facts.value: 60% of the world does not have Internet connectivity

today: RFC 7962 is an Informational document and documents the emerging field of alternative network deployments. As of 2016, mature networks like guifi.net demonstrated viability at scale with thousands of nodes. The framework and taxonomy it provides remain useful for understanding how communities and organizations build connectivity infrastructure outside commercial models.

sections.title: What Are Alternative Networks
sections.content:
Alternative networks are locally owned or community-managed Internet access systems that differ from mainstream commercial networks. Mainstream networks are typically large, centralized services run by a single company where users pay a subscription fee. Alternative networks, by contrast, may be smaller in scale, governed collectively, share infrastructure costs, and often rely on users contributing their own equipment and expertise.

These networks emerged over the last decade to solve real problems: lack of Internet access in rural and remote areas, high costs in underserved communities, and desire for local control and governance. They use predominantly wireless technologies (because unlicensed spectrum is cheap) but may also use wired fiber in some cases.
sections.eli5: Alternative networks are built by communities or groups instead of big companies. They can be smaller, cheaper, and run the way local people want them to be run.

sections.title: Types of Alternative Networks
sections.content:
Community Networks are the most decentralized type. They are self-managed, grow organically as new members join and contribute equipment, and use participatory governance. Members typically keep ownership of their own equipment or contribute it to the commons. Examples include guifi.net in Spain and various Freifunk networks in Germany.

Wireless Internet Service Providers (WISPs) are commercially operated but designed for areas mainstream ISPs do not serve. A company deploys the infrastructure and provides service for a fee. They typically use wireless point-to-multipoint links on unlicensed spectrum but may use licensed frequencies in regions where unlicensed spectrum is crowded.

The Shared Infrastructure Model occurs when a community owns or has deployed infrastructure but rents capacity to an operator. The operator provides Internet service and handles management; the community receives some income to help offset network costs. This happens in rural areas where a community network is backhaul for a commercial service.

Crowdshared Approaches are networks where users share their home Wi-Fi capacity. Special routers create two networks: one for the owner and one public. A Virtual Network Operator (VNO) coordinates the service, handling authentication and payments. Companies like Fon implement this model.

Rural Utility Cooperatives use the cooperative model common for rural electricity. A cooperative owns and operates broadband infrastructure, often fiber, and provides service to its members. This approach is growing in the United States where rural electric cooperatives have discovered fiber lines installed for smart-grid purposes can also carry Internet.

Testbeds for Research are networks built by academic or research entities to study networking technologies. Some begin as centralized but evolve toward community governance as local stakeholders become involved.
sections.eli5: Alternative networks come in different flavors. Some are run entirely by the community, some by a business for underserved areas, some where communities rent to an operator, some where people share their home Wi-Fi, and some run by rural cooperatives or researchers.

sections.title: Technologies Used
sections.content:
The vast majority of alternative networks use wireless technologies because standard equipment is inexpensive and unlicensed spectrum is freely available. Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) is the most common, using both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands. Some networks use the 2.4 GHz band for local access and 5 GHz for longer backbone links between neighborhoods. Wi-Fi is designed for short distances, but vendors offer alternative MAC protocols (usually based on Time Division Multiple Access, or TDMA) for long-distance links reaching over 100 kilometers.

Mobile technologies like GSM are also deployed, enabled by open-source projects such as OpenBTS and OpenBSC. These allow voice, SMS, and Internet services over alternative networks with an IP backhaul. The field is trending toward 4G and 5G integration for higher data rates.

Dynamic Spectrum Solutions including TV White Spaces (unused television frequencies) are emerging. IEEE 802.11af (White-Fi) and IEEE 802.22 are standards for this. They use cognitive radio to detect and avoid interference with primary users, enabling rural coverage at ranges up to 100 kilometers with 802.22.

Wired technologies like optical fiber are used in some communities, especially where villagers have laid fiber themselves when commercial providers declined to serve them. This is less common than wireless but growing, particularly among cooperatives.
sections.eli5: Most alternative networks use Wi-Fi because it is cheap and the spectrum is free. Some use phone technologies (GSM, 4G), TV white spaces with special radios, or fiber optic cable dug by the community.

sections.title: How They Operate
sections.content:
Alternative networks use a mix of routing protocols to move traffic. Community networks often use mesh routing protocols like OLSR (Optimized Link State Routing), B.A.T.M.A.N. Advanced, and Babel, which allow packets to hop between routers to find a path. Larger networks use traditional protocols like BGP or OSPF. Some networks run multiple protocols in parallel, using mesh protocols within neighborhoods and traditional routing between them.

Most alternative networks use private IPv4 addresses (from RFC 1918) for lower cost and simplicity, although some are transitioning to IPv6. IP addressing is typically coordinated by a minimal governance infrastructure to avoid conflicts.

Alternative networks provide a range of services including web browsing, email, VoIP with SIP, P2P file sharing, DNS, online gaming, and weather monitoring. Some provide specialized services like community portals, network monitoring tools, and sensor networks. Traffic management is important in networks that share resources among many users; techniques like Active Queue Management (AQM) with Less-than-Best-Effort (LBE) policies protect individual sharers from heavy traffic from other users.
sections.eli5: Alternative networks use special routing protocols to send data through multiple hops. They use free IP addresses, provide basic Internet services, and manage traffic fairly when bandwidth is shared among many people.

sections.title: Benefits and Challenges
sections.content:
Alternative networks provide real benefits in underserved areas and communities. They extend Internet access where commercial providers see no profit, enable affordable access, reduce infrastructure costs by spreading them among participants, and foster community participation in network design and operation. They also enable experimentation with alternative governance models, raise awareness of network neutrality issues, and provide critical services during natural disasters.

However, they face persistent challenges. Rural areas struggle with low population density, lack of trained technicians, harsh environments that damage equipment, and insufficient power supply. Networks require ongoing volunteer effort or governance structures to sustain them. Most alternative networks started around 2000 and still predominantly use IPv4, so migrating to IPv6 presents a challenge. Despite these obstacles, the success of mature networks like guifi.net, which has grown exponentially over a decade, demonstrates that alternative networks are a viable model for bringing connectivity to people and communities.
sections.eli5: These networks help people who big companies will not serve and let communities control their own infrastructure. The hard part is keeping them going and dealing with broken equipment in remote places.
